title: EE0848 Machine Learning for SP
section: From Linear Models to Neural Networks
text:
From Linear Models to Neural Networks


What we’ve done so far:

Linear/Logistic Regression: \(y = w^T x + b\)
Works well when data is linearly separable
Feature engineering required for complex patterns

The problem:

Many real-world patterns are non-linear
Manual feature engineering doesn’t scale
We need models that learn representations

The solution:

Stack multiple layers of linear transformations
Add non-linear activations between them
Let the network learn its own features





A simple neural network





Think about what we’ve been doing so far. Logistic regression draws a straight line (or hyperplane) to separate classes. If the data isn’t linearly separable, we had to manually engineer features — polynomial features, interaction terms, etc. Neural networks automate this: each layer learns a transformation of the data, and by stacking layers with non-linear activations, the network can learn arbitrarily complex decision boundaries. The key insight: a neural network is just a composition of simple functions.

Versatile: same architecture can model images, text, audio, time series
Automatic feature learning: no manual feature engineering
Scalable: performance improves with more data and compute
Foundation for Deep Learning (CNNs, RNNs, Transformers…)

Different neural network architectures





Neural networks are not universally better — for small datasets, a random forest or XGBoost will often beat a neural network. The advantage of neural networks comes with scale: more data, more compute, more complex patterns. And they’re incredibly versatile — the same basic architecture can handle images, text, audio, and structured data. The architectures shown here — feedforward, convolutional, recurrent, transformer — are all built from the same basic building blocks we’ll learn today.

title: EE0848 Machine Learning for SP
text:
A Signal-Processing View


One hidden layer = a bank of learned filters.
For input \(x \in \mathbb{R}^n\), layer 1 computes: \[h_j = f\big(w_j^T x + b_j\big), \quad j = 1, \ldots, m\]

Each row \(w_j\) of \(W_1\) is a filter / template
\(w_j^T x\) is an inner product — exactly a matched-filter response
\(f(\cdot)\) is a non-linear detector (threshold / rectifier)
Depth → hierarchical feature extraction (cf. multi-resolution analysis)

What’s new vs. classical SP? The filters are learned from data, not hand-designed from a basis (Fourier, wavelet, Gabor…).




Classical SP
Neural Network




Fixed basis (DFT, DWT)
Learned basis (\(W_1\))


Matched filter
\(w_j^T x\) + activation


Thresholding
ReLU / step


Multi-resolution
Depth / hierarchy


Linear + detector
Composition of both



Neural networks generalize the SP toolkit: instead of choosing a filter bank, you learn one tailored to your task.



Before we dive into the details, I want to give you a signal-processing perspective on what a neural network actually is. Look at the first hidden layer: each neuron computes w_j transpose x, which is literally an inner product — a matched filter response. The activation function is a non-linear detector, just like thresholding. So one hidden layer is a bank of learned matched filters followed by non-linear detectors. The weight matrix W1 is a learned basis. When we stack layers, we get hierarchical feature extraction — very similar to multi-resolution analysis with wavelets. The key difference from classical SP: instead of choosing the Fourier basis, a wavelet basis, or a Gabor dictionary ahead of time, the network learns the basis that’s best for your specific task. This is the modern view of deep learning from a signal processing standpoint.

title: EE0848 Machine Learning for SP
text:
The Perceptron (1958)



Simplest neural network — models a single neuron
Introduced by Frank Rosenblatt at Cornell
Hardware implementation: the Mark I Perceptron

How it works:

Take inputs \(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n\)
Multiply each by a weight \(w_i\)
Add a bias \(b\)
Apply an activation function

\[z = \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i x_i + b = w^T x + b\] \[y = f(z)\]
Look familiar? It’s logistic regression with a different activation!




Frank Rosenblatt with the Perceptron





The perceptron was invented in 1958 by Frank Rosenblatt. It’s literally a single neuron: take some inputs, multiply by weights, add them up, and apply a threshold function. Notice something? The weighted sum part — w transpose x plus b — is exactly what linear regression and logistic regression compute. The only difference is what happens after: logistic regression applies a sigmoid, the original perceptron applies a step function. So you already understand the core computation of a neural network.

\[ f(z) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } z \ge 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } z < 0 \end{cases} \]




Diagram of a single Perceptron unit





Here’s the anatomy of a perceptron. The inputs are your features — pixel values, sensor readings, whatever. Each input gets multiplied by a weight that says “how important is this input?” The bias shifts the decision boundary, just like the intercept in linear regression. We compute the weighted sum z, then pass it through an activation function. The original perceptron used a hard step function — output 1 if z is positive, 0 otherwise. This gives a binary classifier with a linear decision boundary.

text:
Perceptron: Learning Rule
The perceptron learns by adjusting weights based on errors:
\[w_i^{\text{new}} = w_i^{\text{old}} + \eta \cdot (y_{\text{true}} - y_{\text{pred}}) \cdot x_i\] \[b^{\text{new}} = b^{\text{old}} + \eta \cdot (y_{\text{true}} - y_{\text{pred}})\]



Scenario
\(y_{\text{true}} - y_{\text{pred}}\)
Update




Correct prediction
0

Predicted 0, should be 1
+1

Predicted 1, should be 0
−1

\(\eta\) = learning rate (small step size, e.g. 0.01)
Convergence theorem: if data is linearly separable, the perceptron will find a separating hyperplane in finite steps


The learning rule is intuitive: if the prediction is correct, do nothing. If we predicted 0 but the answer was 1, increase the weights so that similar inputs push the output higher next time. If we predicted 1 but the answer was 0, decrease them. The learning rate eta controls how big each adjustment is. There’s a beautiful theorem: if the data is linearly separable, the perceptron learning algorithm is guaranteed to converge. But that’s also its limitation — what if the data isn’t linearly separable?

No single line can separate the 0s from the 1s!
This limitation caused the first “AI winter” — funding dried up because people thought neural networks were fundamentally limited.
Solution: stack multiple perceptrons → Multilayer Perceptron

AND (linearly separable):
  x2

This is the famous XOR problem. AND is easy — draw a line and you can separate the positives from the negatives. But XOR? The positives are at (0,1) and (1,0), the negatives at (0,0) and (1,1). No single straight line can separate them. Minsky and Papert proved this in 1969 and it basically killed neural network research for over a decade. But the fix was already known in principle: use multiple layers. Two perceptrons in a hidden layer can each draw a line, and the output perceptron combines them. The problem was training — we didn’t have an efficient algorithm for learning the hidden layer weights until backpropagation was popularized in 1986.

Geometric view:
The hidden layer draws two lines in input space. Together they carve the plane into regions. The output layer picks the region where \(h_1=1, h_2=0\).
  x2
  1 | ✓   ✗
    |  ╲ ╲        ← two lines

Moral: depth lets the network build complex boundaries by composing simple pieces.



Let me make this concrete. The XOR can be rewritten: it’s 1 exactly when x1 or x2 is 1, AND when they’re not both 1. Two linear pieces. So we use two hidden neurons — each draws one line. h1 computes OR by firing whenever x1+x2 is at least 1. h2 computes AND by firing only when x1+x2 is at least 2. The output neuron then computes h1 AND NOT h2. Trace through the truth table: for input (1,1), h1=1, h2=1, so h1 AND NOT h2 = 0. For (1,0) or (0,1), h1=1 and h2=0, so output is 1. This is the essence of what depth does: each hidden neuron carves a half-plane, and subsequent layers compose these into arbitrary regions. We constructed these weights by hand; backprop learns them automatically.

title: EE0848 Machine Learning for SP
text:
Multilayer Perceptron (MLP)



Stack multiple layers of neurons
Feedforward: data flows Input → Hidden → Output
Each hidden layer learns increasingly abstract representations

Structure:



Layer
Role




Input
Receives raw features (\(x\))


Hidden (1 or more)
Learn intermediate representations


Output
Produces final prediction



Key requirement: non-linear activation between layers! Otherwise multiple linear layers collapse to one.




Multilayer Perceptron structure





An MLP has three types of layers. The input layer just receives the features — it doesn’t do any computation. The hidden layers are where the magic happens: each neuron computes a weighted sum and applies a non-linear activation. The output layer produces the final prediction. You can have as many hidden layers as you want — more layers means the network can learn more complex patterns. But there’s a critical requirement: you must have non-linear activations between layers. If you stack linear layers without activations, the entire network reduces to a single linear transformation. That’s just linear regression with extra steps!

Let me write out the math explicitly. The input x goes through a linear transformation — multiply by weight matrix W1, add bias b1 — then through a non-linear activation f1. That gives us the hidden representation h. Then h goes through another linear transformation and activation to produce the output y. The whole thing is a composition of simple functions: linear, non-linear, linear, non-linear. The weight matrices are what we learn during training. W1 has shape (hidden_size × input_size) and W2 has shape (output_size × hidden_size).

title: EE0848 Machine Learning for SP
text:
Universal Approximation Theorem

An MLP with one hidden layer containing enough neurons can approximate any continuous function to arbitrary precision.



What this means:

Neural networks are extremely powerful function approximators
In theory, a single hidden layer is sufficient
The hidden layer needs a non-linear activation

What this does NOT mean:

We can always find the right weights (training is hard)
A single hidden layer is practical (may need astronomically many neurons)
Deeper is not better (in practice, deeper networks learn more efficiently)


Why depth helps in practice:

Deep networks learn hierarchical features

Layer 1: simple patterns
Layer 2: combinations of simple patterns
Layer 3: complex structures

Exponentially more efficient than a single wide layer
Each layer builds on the previous one




The Universal Approximation Theorem is one of the most important results in neural network theory. It says that a single hidden layer MLP with enough neurons and a non-linear activation can approximate any continuous function. That’s incredible — it means neural networks are universal function approximators. But there’s a catch: “enough neurons” could mean an astronomically large number. In practice, deeper networks with fewer neurons per layer are much more efficient than a single huge hidden layer. Why? Because depth allows the network to learn hierarchical representations — simple features first, then combinations, then complex structures. This compositionality is much more parameter-efficient than trying to learn everything in one shot.

title: EE0848 Machine Learning for SP
text:
Why Activation Functions?
Without non-linearity, stacking layers is pointless:
\[W_2 \cdot (W_1 x + b_1) + b_2 = (W_2 W_1) x + (W_2 b_1 + b_2) = W' x + b'\]
Two linear layers = one linear layer. No gain from depth!
Requirements for a good activation function:







Requirement
Why




Non-linear
Enables complex decision boundaries


Differentiable
Needed for gradient-based training


Efficient gradients
Avoid vanishing/exploding gradients


Computationally cheap
Applied to every neuron, every forward pass






Common activation functions



This is the most important thing to understand about activation functions. If I stack two linear layers without an activation in between, I can always simplify them into a single linear layer — just multiply the two weight matrices. So depth gives you nothing without non-linearity. The activation function is what makes a neural network more than a fancy linear model. We need it to be non-linear (obviously), differentiable (because we train with gradient descent), have well-behaved gradients (not too small, not too large), and be cheap to compute (because we call it millions of times).

title: EE0848 Machine Learning for SP
text:
Sigmoid


\[\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}\]
Range: \((0, 1)\) — outputs look like probabilities
Derivative: \(\sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)(1 - \sigma(z))\)
Pros:

Smooth, differentiable everywhere
Output interpretable as probability

Cons:

Vanishing gradients: max derivative is 0.25 (at \(z=0\)). After several layers, gradients shrink exponentially → deep layers barely learn.
Not zero-centered: outputs always positive → zig-zag gradient updates
Expensive: requires exp() computation





Sigmoid function and its derivative




Use today: output layer for binary classification only. Rarely in hidden layers.

Sigmoid was the original activation function for neural networks. It squashes any real number into the range (0,1), which is nice for probabilities. But it has a fatal flaw for deep networks: the maximum value of its derivative is only 0.25. When you multiply gradients through multiple layers during backpropagation, you’re multiplying numbers less than 0.25 over and over. After 5-6 layers, the gradient is essentially zero — the early layers can’t learn. This is the vanishing gradient problem, and it’s the main reason why sigmoid is no longer used in hidden layers. We still use it in the output layer for binary classification, where we need a probability.

title: EE0848 Machine Learning for SP
text:
Tanh


\[\tanh(z) = \frac{e^{z} - e^{-z}}{e^{z} + e^{-z}}\]
Range: \((-1, 1)\) — zero-centered
Derivative: \(\tanh'(z) = 1 - \tanh^2(z)\)
Pros:

Zero-centered → better gradient flow
Stronger gradients than sigmoid (max derivative = 1)

Cons:

Still suffers from vanishing gradients (saturates at extremes)
Still requires exp() computation

Relation to sigmoid: \(\tanh(z) = 2\sigma(2z) - 1\)




Tanh function and its derivative




Use today: sometimes in RNNs/LSTMs. Mostly replaced by ReLU in feedforward nets.

Tanh is the “improved sigmoid.” Its output is centered at zero, which helps gradient descent converge faster — the updates don’t zig-zag as much. Its maximum derivative is 1, which is four times larger than sigmoid’s 0.25. But it still saturates: for very large or very small inputs, the derivative approaches zero. So deep networks with tanh still suffer from vanishing gradients, just less severely than with sigmoid. Tanh is still used in some recurrent networks, but for standard feedforward networks, ReLU is the default.

title: EE0848 Machine Learning for SP
text:
ReLU: The Modern Standard


\[\text{ReLU}(z) = \max(0, z)\]
Range: \([0, \infty)\)
Derivative: \(\text{ReLU}'(z) = \begin{cases} 1 & z > 0 \\ 0 & z \le 0 \end{cases}\)
Pros:

No vanishing gradient for \(z > 0\) (derivative = 1)
Computationally trivial: just a threshold
Promotes sparsity: many neurons output exactly 0
Fast convergence: ~6× faster than sigmoid (Krizhevsky, 2012)

Cons:

“Dying ReLU”: if \(z < 0\) always, neuron permanently outputs 0
Not zero-centered





ReLU function and its derivative





ReLU is the activation function that made deep learning work. It’s embarrassingly simple: return z if z is positive, return 0 otherwise. The key advantage: for positive inputs, the derivative is exactly 1. No matter how many layers you stack, the gradient doesn’t shrink when flowing through ReLU neurons — that’s why deep networks can actually train. It’s also incredibly fast — just a comparison operation, no exponentials. The downside is the “dying ReLU” problem: if a neuron always receives negative inputs, its gradient is always zero, and it never recovers. This is addressed by variants like Leaky ReLU.

Variant
Formula

ReLU

Leaky ReLU

No dead neurons (small negative slope)


ELU
\(z\) if \(z>0\), else \(\alpha(e^z - 1)\)
Smooth, zero-centered for negative inputs


GELU

Smooth, self-gated; used in modern CNNs



Rule of thumb: start with ReLU. Try Leaky ReLU if you suspect dying neurons.

Several variants of ReLU have been proposed to address the dying neuron problem. Leaky ReLU adds a small slope for negative inputs — instead of zero, you get alpha times z, where alpha is typically 0.01. This means the gradient is never completely zero, so neurons can always recover. ELU is smooth and approaches negative alpha for very negative inputs, which pushes the mean activation closer to zero. GELU and Swish are smooth approximations of ReLU that have become popular in Transformers and modern architectures. For most practical purposes, plain ReLU works fine. Use Leaky ReLU if you notice dead neurons during training.

title: EE0848 Machine Learning for SP
text:
Softmax: Multi-class Output


For \(C\) classes with raw scores (logits) \(z_1, \ldots, z_C\):
\[\text{softmax}(z)_i = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{C} e^{z_j}}\]
Properties:

Each output \(\in (0, 1)\), all outputs sum to 1 → valid probability distribution
Exponential amplifies differences — the largest logit dominates
Generalizes sigmoid to \(C\) classes (sigmoid is softmax with \(C=2\))

Numerical stability: subtract the max before exponentiating: \[\text{softmax}(z)_i = \frac{e^{z_i - \max_j z_j}}{\sum_k e^{z_k - \max_j z_j}}\]
Otherwise \(e^{z_i}\) can overflow for large logits.

Example (3 classes, logits \(z = [2, 1, 0]\)):

Important


In PyTorch, nn.CrossEntropyLoss applies softmax internally (log-sum-exp trick). Your model outputs raw logits — no softmax in forward().






Softmax is the standard output activation for multi-class classification. It takes a vector of raw scores — called logits — and converts them to a probability distribution. The formula is simple: exponentiate each logit and divide by the sum. The exponential has two effects: it ensures all outputs are positive, and it amplifies differences — a logit that’s just slightly larger than the others will get most of the probability mass. Softmax is literally the multi-class generalization of sigmoid. There’s one numerical issue: if your logits are large, e to the z can overflow. The fix is to subtract the maximum logit before exponentiating — this doesn’t change the result but keeps everything bounded. In practice, you never write softmax by hand. PyTorch’s CrossEntropyLoss applies softmax internally using the log-sum-exp trick, which is numerically stable. So your model outputs raw logits, not probabilities. This is a very common source of bugs: students apply softmax in the model AND use CrossEntropyLoss, which double-applies it.

title: EE0848 Machine Learning for SP
text:
Loss Functions
The loss function measures how far the model’s predictions are from the true values:








Task
Loss Function
Formula




Regression
Mean Squared Error (MSE)
\(L = \frac{1}{N}\sum(y - \hat{y})^2\)


Binary classification
Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE)
\(L = -\frac{1}{N}\sum[y\log\hat{y} + (1-y)\log(1-\hat{y})]\)


Multi-class
Cross-Entropy
\(L = -\frac{1}{N}\sum\sum y_c \log \hat{y}_c\)



The goal of training: find weights \(\theta = (W, b)\) that minimize the loss:
\[\theta^* = \arg\min_\theta L(\theta)\]

Before we can train, we need to define what “good” means. The loss function quantifies the error. For regression, MSE is the standard — it penalizes large errors quadratically. For binary classification, binary cross-entropy measures how well predicted probabilities match the true labels. For multi-class classification, cross-entropy generalizes BCE. The key idea: training is an optimization problem. We want to find the weights that minimize the loss over the training data. We solve this with gradient descent.

title: EE0848 Machine Learning for SP
text:
Gradient Descent: Intuition


Idea: move weights in the direction that decreases the loss
\[\theta^{\text{new}} = \theta^{\text{old}} - \eta \cdot \nabla_\theta L\]

\(\nabla_\theta L\) = gradient (direction of steepest increase)
\(\eta\) = learning rate (step size)
We go opposite to the gradient → downhill

Learning rate matters:



\(\eta\) too small
\(\eta\) too large




Very slow convergence
Overshoots, diverges


May get stuck in bad local minima
Loss oscillates or increases


Safe but wasteful
Fast but unstable




Variants:



Method
Batch Size
Trade-off




Batch GD
All data
Stable but slow


SGD
1 sample
Fast but noisy


Mini-batch SGD
32–256
Best of both



Mini-batch SGD is the standard in practice — fast updates with reasonable gradient estimates.



Gradient descent is the core optimization algorithm. The gradient of the loss tells us the direction in which the loss increases fastest. We want to decrease the loss, so we move in the opposite direction. The learning rate controls how big each step is — too small and training takes forever, too large and we overshoot the minimum and bounce around. In practice, we use mini-batch SGD: instead of computing the gradient over the entire dataset (expensive) or a single sample (noisy), we use a batch of 32 to 256 samples. This gives us a good gradient estimate while being computationally efficient, and the noise from random batches actually helps escape local minima.

title: EE0848 Machine Learning for SP
text:
Backpropagation: How NNs Learn


Problem: we need \(\frac{\partial L}{\partial w}\) for every weight in the network.
Backpropagation computes all gradients efficiently using the chain rule:
\[\frac{\partial L}{\partial w} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial y} \cdot \frac{\partial y}{\partial z} \cdot \frac{\partial z}{\partial w}\]
The process:

Forward pass: compute predictions layer by layer
Compute loss: compare prediction to target
Backward pass: propagate gradients from output back to input
Update: adjust weights using the gradients





The backpropagation algorithm





Backpropagation is the algorithm that makes training neural networks practical. The key insight is that you can compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every single weight in the network efficiently by applying the chain rule layer by layer, starting from the output and working backwards. Forward pass: data flows through the network, and we save the intermediate values. Backward pass: the error gradient flows back through the network, and at each layer we compute how much each weight contributed to the error. This is where the name comes from — we’re propagating errors backward. The beauty is that this is computationally efficient: the backward pass has roughly the same cost as the forward pass.

title: EE0848 Machine Learning for SP
text:
Chain Rule: Worked Example
Setup: single neuron, weight \(w\), bias \(b=0\), sigmoid activation, squared error loss.
\[x \xrightarrow{w} z = wx \xrightarrow{\sigma} y = \sigma(z) \xrightarrow{L} L = \tfrac{1}{2}(y - y_{\text{true}})^2\]
Chain rule: \[\frac{\partial L}{\partial w} = \underbrace{\frac{\partial L}{\partial y}}_{y - y_{\text{true}}} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{\partial y}{\partial z}}_{\sigma'(z) = y(1-y)} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{\partial z}{\partial w}}_{x}\]
Numerical example: \(x = 2\), \(w = 0.5\), \(y_{\text{true}} = 1\)

−0.106



Gradient is negative → increase \(w\) to decrease loss.

Let me trace through a complete example. We have a single neuron: input x=2, weight w=0.5. Forward pass: z = 0.5 times 2 = 1.0. Apply sigmoid: y = sigma(1) = 0.731. The true label is 1, so the loss is 0.5 times (0.731 - 1) squared = 0.036. Now the backward pass. We need three derivatives and multiply them: dL/dy is (y - y_true) = -0.269. dy/dz is sigma’(z) = y(1-y) = 0.197. dz/dw is just x = 2. Multiply them all: -0.269 times 0.197 times 2 = -0.106. The negative gradient tells us: to decrease the loss, we should increase w. So the weight update moves w from 0.5 toward a larger value.

title: EE0848 Machine Learning for SP
text:
Backpropagation: Code


Forward pass:
import numpy as np

def sigmoid(z):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

# Layer 1 (Hidden)
z1 = np.dot(X, W1) + b1
a1 = sigmoid(z1)

# Layer 2 (Output)
z2 = np.dot(a1, W2) + b2
a2 = sigmoid(z2)

# Error
error = a2 - y  # (prediction - target)

Backward pass + update:
def sigmoid_deriv(a):
    return a * (1 - a)

# Output layer gradients
# Shortcut: sigmoid' * BCE' telescopes to (y_hat - y).
# For MSE or other losses you MUST multiply by sigmoid_deriv(a2).
delta2 = error
grad_W2 = np.dot(a1.T, delta2)
grad_b2 = np.sum(delta2, axis=0)

# Hidden layer gradients
delta1 = np.dot(delta2, W2.T) * sigmoid_deriv(a1)
grad_W1 = np.dot(X.T, delta1)
grad_b1 = np.sum(delta1, axis=0)

# Update parameters
W1 -= lr * grad_W1;  b1 -= lr * grad_b1
W2 -= lr * grad_W2;  b2 -= lr * grad_b2








Note


In practice, you never write this manually. PyTorch’s autograd does it automatically — just call loss.backward().




Here’s the full backpropagation in NumPy for a 2-layer network. The forward pass computes activations layer by layer. The backward pass computes gradients in reverse order: first the output layer gradients, then we propagate them back to get the hidden layer gradients. Then we update all weights. This is educational, but I want to be clear: you will never implement backpropagation manually in practice. PyTorch’s autograd system does all of this automatically. You define the forward pass, call loss.backward(), and all the gradients are computed for you. But understanding what’s happening under the hood helps you debug training issues.

Optimizers: Beyond Basic SGD








Optimizer
Update Rule
Key Feature




SGD
\(\theta \gets \theta - \eta \nabla L\)
Simple baseline


SGD + Momentum
\(v \gets \beta v + \nabla L\); \(\theta \gets \theta - \eta v\)
Smooths updates, accelerates


RMSprop
Adapts LR per-parameter by gradient magnitude
Handles different scales


Adam
Momentum + adaptive LR (1st + 2nd moment)
Most popular default


AdamW
Adam + decoupled weight decay
Better generalization



Adam is the default choice for most tasks:

Combines benefits of momentum and adaptive learning rates
Less sensitive to learning rate choice
Works well “out of the box” with \(\text{lr} = 10^{-3}\)


Plain SGD works, but it has issues: the gradient can be noisy, and all parameters use the same learning rate even though some might need larger or smaller steps. Momentum smooths out the noise by accumulating a running average of past gradients — like a ball rolling downhill with inertia. RMSprop adapts the learning rate for each parameter based on how large its recent gradients have been. Adam combines both ideas: it uses momentum for the gradient direction and adaptive scaling for the step size. AdamW is Adam with a subtle fix for weight decay that works better in practice. For most problems, start with Adam or AdamW at learning rate 1e-3 — it’s a solid default.

title: EE0848 Machine Learning for SP
text:
The Vanishing Gradient Problem


Problem: gradients shrink exponentially as they flow backward through many layers.
For a network with \(L\) layers using sigmoid (\(\sigma'_{\max} = 0.25\)):
\[\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_1} \propto \prod_{l=1}^{L} \sigma'(z_l) \le 0.25^L\]



Layers
Max gradient factor




2
\(0.25^2 = 0.0625\)


5
\(0.25^5 \approx 0.001\)


10
\(0.25^{10} \approx 10^{-6}\)



Early layers stop learning!

Solutions:

ReLU activation (derivative = 1 for \(z > 0\))
Batch Normalization (stabilize activations)
Skip connections (ResNet — gradient shortcuts)
Proper initialization (He, Xavier)
Gradient clipping (cap gradient magnitude)




This is the single biggest challenge in training deep networks. When you multiply the gradient through many sigmoid activations, each one scales it down by at most 0.25. After 10 layers, the gradient is a millionth of what it was at the output — the early layers effectively can’t learn. This is why deep networks with sigmoid were impossible to train in the 1990s. The solutions we have today: ReLU doesn’t squash gradients for positive inputs (derivative is 1). Batch normalization keeps activations in a well-behaved range. Skip connections in ResNet let the gradient bypass layers entirely. And proper weight initialization ensures we start in a good region. Together, these techniques enable training networks with hundreds of layers.

title: EE0848 Machine Learning for SP
text:
Data Normalization
Scale input features so they’re on a comparable range:








Method
Formula
Result




Min-Max
\(x' = \frac{x - \min}{\max - \min}\)
Scale to \([0, 1]\)


Standardization
\(x' = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\)
Scale to \(\mu=0, \sigma=1\)



Why it matters for neural networks:

Unscaled features → some weights get huge gradients, others get tiny ones
Optimizer struggles to find a good learning rate for all weights
Standardized data → loss landscape is more spherical → easier optimization


Fit the scaler on training data only! Apply the same transform to validation/test. Otherwise you leak future information.


We covered normalization before, but it’s even more important for neural networks than for classical ML. When features have very different scales, the loss landscape becomes elongated — the gradient points mostly in the direction of the large-scale features, and the optimizer oscillates instead of converging. Standardizing the data makes the landscape more spherical, which helps gradient descent find the minimum much faster. The golden rule: fit the scaler on training data, then apply it to validation and test data. Never compute statistics on test data — that would be data leakage.

title: EE0848 Machine Learning for SP
text:
Weight Initialization
How you set the initial weights matters enormously:
Why not zeros? All neurons compute the same thing → all get the same gradient → all stay the same. Symmetry is never broken.
Why not large random? Activations saturate → vanishing gradients from the start.








Strategy
Formula
Best for




Small random
\(N(0, 0.01)\)
Simple, but often suboptimal


Xavier / Glorot
\(\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{2}{n_{\text{in}} + n_{\text{out}}}}\)
Sigmoid, Tanh


He (Kaiming)
\(\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{2}{n_{\text{in}}}}\)
ReLU (default in PyTorch)




\(n_{\text{in}}\): number of inputs to the layer
Biases: initialized to zero (asymmetry comes from weights)


Initialization sounds boring but it’s critical. If you initialize all weights to zero, every neuron in a layer computes the exact same output, gets the exact same gradient, and stays identical forever — the network can never learn different features. So we need randomness. But the scale of the random values matters: too large and activations saturate, too small and signals vanish. Xavier initialization was designed for sigmoid and tanh: it sets the variance so that signal magnitude is preserved through layers. He initialization does the same for ReLU, accounting for the fact that ReLU kills half the activations. In PyTorch, He initialization is the default for linear layers, so you usually don’t need to worry about it.

text:
Overfitting in Neural Networks
Neural networks have millions of parameters — they can memorize the training data.
Signs of overfitting:

Training loss keeps decreasing
Validation loss starts increasing
Large gap between training and validation accuracy

Remedies:



Technique
How it helps




More data
Best solution, but not always available


Dropout
Randomly zero neurons → prevents co-adaptation


Weight decay (L2)
Penalizes large weights → simpler model


Early stopping
Stop when validation loss rises


Data augmentation
Artificially increase data diversity


Batch normalization
Slight regularization effect


Simpler architecture
Fewer layers / neurons




Overfitting is the number one practical problem with neural networks. A network with enough parameters can memorize the entire training set — achieving near-zero training loss while being terrible on new data. The telltale sign is the validation loss curve: it goes down initially (learning), then turns and starts going up (overfitting). The solutions are the same ones we’ve discussed throughout the course — regularization in various forms — plus some NN-specific ones like dropout and batch normalization. In practice, you’ll use several of these simultaneously. We’ll cover dropout and data augmentation in detail next week when we build CNNs.

By stacking perceptrons into multilayer networks with non-linear activations, we get universal function approximators. text:
What is a CNN?



Learns filters (kernels) that slide across the input to detect patterns.
Exploits local connectivity + weight sharing → huge parameter savings.
State-of-the-art on images, audio spectrograms, and 1-D sensor signals.
Core inductive biases: locality, weight sharing, translation equivariance.





High-level CNN pipeline





A CNN is not magic — it’s a neural network with a very specific architectural constraint: instead of connecting every neuron to every input, each neuron only looks at a small local patch. The same set of weights (the kernel) is reused at every position. This gives us three things for free: locality (nearby pixels matter more than far-away ones), weight sharing (same filter everywhere), and translation equivariance (if the cat moves, the feature map shifts but doesn’t change shape).

title: EE0848 Machine Learning for SP
text:
Why Convolutions?









Dense Layer
Convolution




Connectivity
Every neuron ↔︎ every pixel → parameter explosion
Filter \(K \times K \times C\) reused across spatial positions


Inductive bias
No assumption about locality
Explicit bias: nearby samples matter most


Translation
Variant — moving an object changes output
Equivariant — shift input → shift output


Params (example)
32×32×3 input → 256 neurons = 786k weights
3×3×3 filter × 256 = 7k weights




This table is the key selling point of CNNs. A single dense layer connecting a 32×32 RGB image to 256 hidden units needs over 786 thousand parameters — and that’s just one layer. A convolutional layer with 256 3×3 filters needs about 7000. That’s over 100× fewer. This is why CNNs can go deep without exploding in parameter count.

title: EE0848 Machine Learning for SP
text:
Discrete Convolution (1-D) Recap
Convolution (DSP definition): \[y[n] = (x * h)[n] = \sum_{m} x[m]\, h[n-m]\]
Cross-correlation (what DL frameworks actually compute): \[ (x \star h)[n] = \sum_{m} x[m]\, h[n+m] \]






Note


The kernel is learned, so the flip doesn’t matter — it’s absorbed into the learned weights. The operation matches your DSP course; what differs is the kernel is trained from data, not hand-designed.




I want to be transparent about a notational subtlety. In signal processing, convolution flips the kernel before sliding. In deep learning, we don’t flip — we do cross-correlation. But since the kernel is learned by gradient descent, it doesn’t matter: if the “correct” kernel should be flipped, the optimizer will just learn the flipped version. So in DL papers and code, people just call it “convolution” even though it’s technically cross-correlation.

Kernel sliding over image grid



Numerical example (3×3 kernel, no padding, stride 1):
\[\text{Input patch} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad \text{Kernel} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\]
\[\text{Output} = \sum_{i,j} \text{input}_{ij} \cdot \text{kernel}_{ij}\] \[= 1{\cdot}1 + 0{\cdot}0 + 1{\cdot}({-1}) + 0{\cdot}1 + 1{\cdot}0 + 0{\cdot}({-1}) + 1{\cdot}1 + 0{\cdot}0 + 1{\cdot}({-1}) = \mathbf{0}\]
Slide the kernel to the next position → next output value.



Let me walk through the computation. We place the kernel on top of a 3×3 patch of the input, multiply element-wise, and sum. Here the kernel is a vertical edge detector: left column is all 1s, right column is all -1s. When placed on a symmetric patch like this one, the output is zero — no vertical edge. If the left side was brighter than the right side, we’d get a positive value. This is exactly how edge detection works in image processing — but in a CNN, we let the network learn what kernels are useful.

text:
Output Size Formula
For a given spatial dimension:
\[\boxed{H_{\text{out}} = \left\lfloor \frac{H_{\text{in}} - K + 2P}{S} \right\rfloor + 1}\]



Symbol
Meaning
Typical values




\(K\)
Kernel size
3, 5, 7


\(P\)
Padding
0 (valid), \(\lfloor K/2 \rfloor\) (same)


\(S\)
Stride
1 (preserve size), 2 (downsample)



Quick examples (input 32×32):

\(K=3, P=1, S=1\) → \(\lfloor(32-3+2)/1\rfloor+1 = 32\) (same)
\(K=3, P=0, S=1\) → \(\lfloor(32-3+0)/1\rfloor+1 = 30\) (shrinks by 2)
\(K=3, P=1, S=2\) → \(\lfloor(32-3+2)/2\rfloor+1 = 16\) (halved)


This is the formula you’ll use most often when designing CNNs. The key intuition: padding=K/2 with stride=1 preserves the spatial size (called “same” padding). Stride=2 halves the size — it’s an alternative to pooling for downsampling. Let’s work through the numbers: 32 minus 3 plus 2 divided by 1, floor, plus 1 = 32. So with padding=1 and a 3×3 kernel, the output stays 32×32.

Stride 2 vs Stride 1, plus zero-padding



Stride:

Stride 1 → kernel moves 1 pixel at a time
Stride 2 → kernel jumps 2 pixels → halves spatial resolution
Larger stride = more aggressive downsampling

Padding:

No padding → output shrinks, borders ignored
Zero-padding → preserves spatial dimensions
“Same” padding: \(P = \lfloor K/2 \rfloor\)




Stride controls how far the kernel jumps between positions. With stride 1, it moves one pixel at a time and you get the largest possible output. With stride 2, it skips every other position, cutting the spatial size in half. Padding adds zeros around the border of the input. Without it, the output is smaller than the input — you lose border information. With “same” padding, the output has the same spatial dimensions as the input, which makes it easy to stack many conv layers without the feature maps shrinking away.

title: EE0848 Machine Learning for SP
text:
Receptive Field





Receptive field stacking



The receptive field is the region of the input that influences a single output neuron.

Layer 1 (3×3 kernel): sees a 3×3 patch
Layer 2 (3×3 kernel): sees a 5×5 patch of the original input
Layer 3: sees 7×7, and so on…

\[R_l = R_{l-1} + (K_l - 1) \prod_{i=1}^{l-1} S_i\]
Why it matters: deeper layers “see” larger portions of the input → can detect higher-level patterns.



This is one of the most important concepts in CNN design. A single neuron in the first conv layer only sees a 3×3 patch — it can detect an edge. But a neuron in layer 2 is computed from a 3×3 patch of layer 1’s output, and each of those was computed from a 3×3 input patch. So layer 2 effectively sees a 5×5 region of the original input. Layer 3 sees 7×7. This is how CNNs build hierarchical representations: small receptive fields detect local features, large receptive fields detect global structure.

This hierarchy emerges automatically from training — we never tell the network to learn edges first. The architecture (local kernels + pooling) naturally encourages this progression from low-level to high-level.




This is perhaps the most beautiful thing about CNNs. Nobody tells the network to learn edge detectors in layer 1 — it discovers that on its own, because edges are the most useful local features for building up higher-level representations. Layer 2 combines edges into textures and corners. Layer 3 combines those into parts of objects. And deep layers recognize whole objects. This was first visualized clearly by Zeiler and Fergus in 2013, and it’s still one of the most intuitive explanations for why deep CNNs work.

text:
Batch Normalization
Center & scale mini-batch activations:
\[\hat{x}_i = \frac{x_i - \mu_B}{\sqrt{\sigma_B^2 + \varepsilon}}, \qquad y_i = \gamma \hat{x}_i + \beta\]


Training:

Compute \(\mu_B\), \(\sigma_B^2\) from the current mini-batch
Learn per-channel scale (\(\gamma\)) and shift (\(\beta\))
Maintain running average of \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\)


Inference:

Use the running average statistics (not batch stats)
This is why model.eval() matters!

Benefits:

Reduces internal covariate shift
Allows higher learning rates
Slight regularization effect




Batch normalization was a game-changer when it was introduced in 2015. The idea is simple: normalize the activations of each layer so they have zero mean and unit variance across the mini-batch. Then let the network learn a scale and shift — so if it wants the activations to be non-zero-mean, it can do that. The key benefit is that it stabilizes the distribution of activations throughout training, which means you can use much larger learning rates and converge faster. One subtlety students often miss: at inference time, you don’t use the current batch statistics — you use the running averages accumulated during training. This is why calling model.eval() is critical.

text:
Model Definition (1/2)
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class a_CNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        # Conv block 1: 3×32×32 → 16×32×32 → pool → 16×16×16
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(3, 16, kernel_size=5, padding=2)
        self.bn1   = nn.BatchNorm2d(16)
        # Conv block 2: 16×16×16 → 32×16×16 → pool → 32×8×8
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(16, 32, kernel_size=5, padding=2)
        self.bn2   = nn.BatchNorm2d(32)
        # Classifier head
        self.fc1   = nn.Linear(32 * 8 * 8, 64)
        self.drop  = nn.Dropout(0.3)
        self.fc2   = nn.Linear(64, 10)
Parameter count: ~145k — compare to a 2-layer FC on same input: ~800k+

Here’s our model definition. Two convolutional blocks, each with conv, batch norm, ReLU, and max pooling. Then a classifier head with one hidden FC layer, dropout, and the output layer. Notice the shape comments: the input is 3×32×32 (RGB CIFAR-10 image). After conv1 with padding=2 and a 5×5 kernel, the spatial size stays at 32×32 but we now have 16 channels. Max pool halves it to 16×16. Conv2 goes from 16 to 32 channels, pool halves to 8×8. Then we flatten: 32×8×8 = 2048 values → FC → 64 → FC → 10 classes. Total about 145k parameters — much fewer than a fully-connected approach.

text:
Model Definition (2/2) — Forward Pass
    def forward(self, x):                      # x: [B, 3, 32, 32]
        x = F.relu(self.bn1(self.conv1(x)))    # → [B, 16, 32, 32]
        x = F.max_pool2d(x, 2)                 # → [B, 16, 16, 16]
        x = F.relu(self.bn2(self.conv2(x)))    # → [B, 32, 16, 16]
        x = F.max_pool2d(x, 2)                 # → [B, 32,  8,  8]
        x = x.flatten(1)                       # → [B, 2048]
        x = self.drop(F.relu(self.fc1(x)))     # → [B, 64]
        return self.fc2(x)                     # → [B, 10] (logits)
The pattern: Conv → BN → ReLU → Pool repeated, then Flatten → FC → Dropout → FC.
Returns logits — softmax is applied inside CrossEntropyLoss.

The forward method shows the data flow explicitly with shapes. Notice the pattern: convolution, batch norm, ReLU activation, max pooling. This pattern repeats twice. Then we flatten the 3D feature maps into a 1D vector, pass through a fully connected layer with ReLU and dropout, and finally the output layer. The output is raw logits — 10 numbers, one per CIFAR-10 class. We don’t apply softmax here because PyTorch’s CrossEntropyLoss does it internally for numerical stability.

opt   = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-4)
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(label_smoothing=0.05)

Three components to set up. The optimizer: AdamW is the go-to for modern deep learning. It’s Adam with decoupled weight decay, which works better than the original Adam with L2 regularization. Learning rate 1e-3 is a good starting point for Adam. The loss function: CrossEntropyLoss combines log-softmax and negative log likelihood in one step, which is more numerically stable than doing them separately. Label smoothing at 0.05 means instead of training on hard targets [1, 0, 0, …], we use soft targets [0.95, 0.005, 0.005, …]. This prevents the model from becoming overconfident.

Cosine annealing: \[\eta_t = \eta_{\min} + \tfrac{1}{2}(\eta_{\max}-\eta_{\min})\left[1+\cos\left(\tfrac{\pi t}{T_{\max}}\right)\right]\]

Behavior

Learning rate scheduling is crucial for good convergence. The idea: start with a high learning rate to explore the loss landscape quickly, then gradually reduce it to fine-tune. Cosine annealing is the most popular choice — it follows a smooth cosine curve from the initial LR down to near zero. No need to pick when to drop the LR like with StepLR. The scheduler’s step() is called once per epoch, after the optimizer’s step().

text:
Training Loop
for epoch in range(20):
    model.train()                          # enable BN + Dropout
    running_loss = 0
    for xb, yb in train_dl:
        xb, yb = xb.to(device), yb.to(device)
        opt.zero_grad()                    # clear old gradients
        loss = loss_fn(model(xb), yb)      # forward + compute loss
        loss.backward()                    # compute gradients
        opt.step()                         # update weights
        running_loss += loss.item()
    sched.step()                           # update learning rate
    print(f"Epoch {epoch}: loss = {running_loss/len(train_dl):.3f}")
Key points:

model.train() → enables BN running-stat updates and Dropout
opt.zero_grad() → PyTorch accumulates gradients by default — must clear them
sched.step() runs once per epoch (not per batch)


This is the standard PyTorch training loop. Every epoch, we iterate over mini-batches. For each batch: zero the gradients, do a forward pass, compute the loss, backpropagate, and update the weights. Three things students commonly forget: first, call model.train() at the start — this enables dropout and batch norm updates. Second, zero_grad() before each batch — PyTorch accumulates gradients by default, which is useful for gradient accumulation but will give you wrong results if you forget to clear them. Third, the scheduler steps once per epoch, not per batch — putting it inside the batch loop is a common bug.

correct, total = 0, 0
with torch.no_grad():                      # no gradient computation → faster
    for xb, yb in test_dl:
        out = model(xb.to(device))
        preds = out.argmax(dim=1)
        correct += (preds == yb.to(device)).sum().item()

model.eval()
torch.no_grad()

Changes BN & Dropout behavior
Disables gradient tracking


Why
Correct inference statistics
Save memory & speed


Without it
Wrong predictions (BN uses batch stats)

Evaluation mode has two parts that students often confuse. model.eval() changes the behavior of certain layers: batch normalization uses the running averages instead of batch statistics, and dropout is turned off. torch.no_grad() is a separate thing — it tells PyTorch not to build the computation graph, which saves memory and speeds up computation. You need both for correct and efficient inference. A common mistake is forgetting model.eval() — your model will still produce outputs, but batch normalization will use the current batch’s statistics instead of the population statistics, leading to inconsistent results.

Transfer Learning


Idea: take a CNN pretrained on a large dataset (ImageNet, 1M+ images) and adapt it to your task.
Two strategies:

Feature extraction — freeze all backbone weights, only train new head
Fine-tuning — unfreeze some/all backbone layers with a smaller LR

Transfer learning is the single most important practical technique in deep learning. Training a CNN from scratch requires millions of images. But if someone already trained a good model on ImageNet, the early layers learned general features — edges, textures, shapes — that are useful for almost any vision task. We can reuse those features and only train a new classification head for our specific task. With just a few hundred images, you can get excellent results this way. Fine-tuning goes a step further: we unfreeze some backbone layers and train them with a very small learning rate, allowing the features to adapt slightly to our domain.

Here’s the history of CNN architectures through the lens of the ImageNet competition. LeNet started it all in 1998 for digit recognition. AlexNet in 2012 was the watershed moment — it showed that GPUs could train deep CNNs on large datasets, achieving a massive jump in accuracy. title: EE0848 Machine Learning for SP
text:
Skip Connections: Why They Matter
Residual block: \(\quad y = F(x) + x\)


The gradient through a residual block: \[\frac{\partial L}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial y}\left(I + \frac{\partial F}{\partial x}\right)\]

Even if \(\frac{\partial F}{\partial x} \to 0\), the gradient still flows through the identity path (\(I\)).
Solves the vanishing gradient problem.
Enables training networks with 100+ layers.
The block only needs to learn the residual \(F(x) = y - x\) — often easier than learning the full mapping.


    x ─────────────────┐
    │                   │
    ▼                   │
  [Conv → BN → ReLU]   │
    │                   │
    ▼                   │
  [Conv → BN]          │
    │                   │
    ▼                   │
    + ◀─────────────────┘
    │
    ▼
   ReLU
    │
    ▼
    y = F(x) + x



Skip connections are the most important architectural innovation in deep learning. The idea is simple: instead of learning a mapping from x to y directly, we learn the difference, the residual F(x) = y minus x. Then the output is F(x) + x. Why does this help? Look at the gradient. Because of the addition with x, the gradient has a direct path through the identity, even if all the conv layers have tiny gradients, the gradient can still flow backward through the skip connection. This is what enabled training 152-layer networks, when before even 20 layers was difficult.

I want to emphasize that CNNs are not just for images. In signal processing, 1-D CNNs are extremely powerful. For audio, you can either convert to a spectrogram (2D) and use a standard image CNN, or apply 1-D convolutions directly on the waveform. For ECG and EEG, 1-D CNNs can detect arrhythmias by learning temporal patterns in the signal. The API in PyTorch is almost identical: just use Conv1d instead of Conv2d, and your input tensor has shape [batch, channels, time] instead of [batch, channels, height, width]. Everything else — padding, stride, batch norm, pooling — works exactly the same way.

text:
Regularization Round-Up








Technique
Purpose
Where / How




Weight Decay (L2)
Penalize large weights
\(L = L_0 + \lambda \lVert w \rVert_2^2\) (in optimizer)


Dropout
Random sub-networks
After FC / late conv layers


Data Augmentation
Enlarge effective dataset
Input pipeline (training only)


Batch Normalization
Stabilize activations
After every conv layer


Label Smoothing
Soften one-hot targets
\(y_i' = (1-\alpha) y_i + \alpha/K\) (in loss)


Early Stopping
Prevent over-training
Monitor validation loss, stop when it rises









Note


In practice, you use all of these together. They are complementary, not competing.




Here’s every regularization technique we’ve discussed in one table. The key insight is that you don’t pick one — you use them all together. Weight decay is built into the optimizer. Batch normalization goes after every conv layer. Dropout goes after FC layers. Data augmentation is in the data pipeline. Label smoothing is in the loss function. And early stopping is your safety net — you monitor validation loss and stop training when it starts going up. Each technique attacks overfitting from a different angle, and they stack well together.

title: EE0848 Machine Learning for SP
text:
Advantages vs. Limitations







Strengths
Limitations




Parameter-efficient (weight sharing)
Data-hungry (need lots of images)


Translation equivariant
Heavy compute for large inputs


Transfer-learning friendly
Not rotation / scale invariant


Learns hierarchical features
Less interpretable than linear models


Works for 1-D, 2-D, 3-D data
Fixed receptive field (no long-range)




Remedies: group-equivariant CNNs (rotations), depthwise-separable convs (MobileNet), attention / transformers for long-range dependencies.


Let’s be honest about what CNNs can and can’t do. They’re excellent at what they do, but they have real limitations. They need a lot of data — though transfer learning mitigates this. They’re equivariant to translation but not to rotation or scale — a flipped cat looks different to a CNN unless you augment for it. And they have a fixed receptive field, so capturing very long-range dependencies requires either very deep networks or very large kernels. This last limitation is exactly what motivates transformers, which we’ll cover next week.

title: EE0848 Machine Learning for SP
text:
Summary

CNN = stack of Conv → BN → ReLU → Pool, topped by a FC head.
Why it works: locality, weight sharing, translation equivariance.
Key formula: \(H_{\text{out}} = \lfloor(H_{\text{in}} - K + 2P)/S\rfloor + 1\)
Training recipe: AdamW + cosine LR + BN + dropout + augmentation.
Scale up: transfer learning from pretrained backbones (don’t train from scratch).
SP relevance: 1-D CNNs on raw signals; 2-D CNNs on spectrograms.


To summarize: CNNs exploit the spatial structure of data through local connectivity and weight sharing. The standard building blocks — conv, batch norm, ReLU, pooling — stack to create hierarchical feature extractors. Training requires careful setup: the right optimizer, learning rate schedule, and regularization. For practical use, start with transfer learning. And remember, CNNs aren’t just for images — they’re a fundamental tool for any grid-structured data, including the 1-D signals we work with in signal processing.

text:
Why Scaling Matters in Machine Learning?
Feature scaling is a preprocessing step where numerical features are transformed to a common scale to prevent variables with larger magnitudes from dominating the model.
Why is Scaling Important?

Many machine learning algorithms rely on distance metrics (e.g., Euclidean distance). If one feature has a much larger range than another, it will disproportionately influence the model.
Without scaling, a feature like salary (ranging from 10,000 to 100,000) can overshadow another feature like age (ranging from 20 to 60).
Normalization (Min-Max Scaling) and Standardization (Z-score Scaling) are two common approaches used to address this issue.

We already covered StandardScaler (z-score) and MinMaxScaler (min-max normalization) in detail. Let’s talk about the other two:
RobustScaler — Uses the median and interquartile range (IQR) instead of the mean and standard deviation:
\[x_{robust} = \frac{x - \text{median}}{Q_3 - Q_1}\]
Because the median and IQR are not affected by extreme values, RobustScaler is much more resistant to outliers than StandardScaler. Notice in the plot that the data spread looks similar to StandardScaler, but the outlier points are less extreme relative to the bulk of the data.
Normalizer — This one is fundamentally different. It operates row-wise (per sample), not column-wise (per feature). It scales each sample individually so that its feature vector has unit norm (L2 by default):
\[\mathbf{x}_{normalized} = \frac{\mathbf{x}}{\|\mathbf{x}\|}\]
This projects every data point onto the unit circle (or unit sphere in higher dimensions). That’s why in the plot all points collapse onto a small arc — they all have the same distance from the origin, only their direction differs. Normalizer is useful when the direction of the feature vector matters more than its magnitude, e.g., in text classification with TF-IDF or when using cosine similarity.
When to use which?

StandardScaler — Your safe default. Works well when features are roughly Gaussian. Required by models that assume zero-mean data (e.g., PCA, SVM with RBF kernel, logistic regression with regularization).
MinMaxScaler — Use when you need a bounded range (e.g., [0, 1]). Needed when the algorithm interprets values as probabilities or pixel intensities (must be in [0,1]), when using activation functions with bounded domains (sigmoid saturates outside ~[−5, 5], tanh outside ~[−3, 3] — unbounded inputs push them into flat regions where gradients vanish), or when mixing features with existing [0,1] data like image pixels. Also useful for sparse data where you want to preserve zeros. Sensitive to outliers — a single extreme value compresses the rest.
RobustScaler — Use when your data has significant outliers that you want to keep (not remove). It scales the bulk of the data well while preventing outliers from distorting the transformation. A good drop-in replacement for StandardScaler on messy, real-world data.
Normalizer — Use when the magnitude of the feature vector is irrelevant and only the direction matters. Typical use cases: text data (TF-IDF vectors), any setting where you’ll use cosine similarity, or when samples have very different scales but similar “profiles.”

Rule of thumb: if in doubt, start with StandardScaler. Switch to RobustScaler if outliers hurt performance, MinMaxScaler if bounded input is required, or Normalizer if you care about relative proportions across features rather than absolute values.

When to drop?

Drop rows — missingness is small (<5%) and random
Drop columns — feature is mostly missing (>40–50%) or unimportant
Don’t drop — small dataset, or missingness is systematic (dropping may introduce bias)



When is dropping appropriate?

Drop rows when the proportion of incomplete samples is very small (e.g., <5% of the dataset) and missingness is random (MCAR — Missing Completely At Random). Losing a few rows won’t meaningfully reduce your training data or bias your model.
Drop columns when a feature is missing for a large fraction of samples (e.g., >40–50%). At that point, any imputation is mostly guesswork and the feature is unlikely to be reliable. Also drop if the feature is redundant or low-importance.
Don’t drop when data is scarce (small dataset — every sample counts), when missingness is systematic/informative (e.g., patients who skipped a medical test might be sicker — dropping them biases the dataset), or when many features each have a few missing values (dropping rows would cascade and you’d lose most of your data).

General rule: If the data is large and missingness is sparse and random, dropping is the simplest and safest approach. Otherwise, impute.

Imputation methods and when to use each:

Mean / Median / Mode Imputation — Your quick-and-dirty baseline. Use when missingness is small, random, and you need something simple. Prefer median over mean when the feature has outliers or is skewed (median is robust). Use mode for categorical features — mode is simply the most frequently occurring value (e.g., [red, blue, red, green, red] → red). You can’t compute a mean or median for non-numeric data, so mode is the categorical equivalent. Avoid when missingness is large — it artificially reduces variance and weakens correlations between features.
Forward/Backward Fill — Use specifically for time-series data where the assumption “the value stays roughly the same over short gaps” is reasonable (e.g., sensor readings, stock prices at short intervals). Don’t use for tabular data with no temporal ordering — it would be meaningless.
kNN Imputation — Use when features are correlated and you have enough samples for meaningful nearest-neighbor lookups. Good when similar samples tend to have similar values. How it works: for a sample with a missing value in feature X, compute distances to all other samples using only the non-missing features, find the k nearest neighbors, then fill the missing value with the mean of those k neighbors’ values for feature X. It uses multiple neighbors (not just one) for robustness. Avoid on very high-dimensional or very large datasets (distance computations become expensive and less meaningful — curse of dimensionality).
Regression / Model-Based Imputation — Use when features have strong predictable relationships (e.g., height and weight). More accurate than mean imputation but risks overfitting: the imputed values may look “too clean” and overstate the true correlation between features.
Multiple Imputation (MICE) — The gold standard when you need statistically rigorous results (e.g., academic research, clinical studies). It generates multiple plausible datasets, accounts for uncertainty in the imputed values, and produces valid confidence intervals. Overkill for a quick ML pipeline but important when inference and p-values matter.
Interpolation — Use for time-series or spatially ordered data where values change smoothly. Linear interpolation for roughly linear trends, spline for smoother curves. Not applicable to unordered tabular data.
Deep Learning (autoencoders, GANs) — Use when the dataset is very large, patterns are complex, and simpler methods underperform. Rarely the first choice due to complexity.

Practical decision guide: Start with mean/median imputation as a baseline. If model performance suffers, try kNN or iterative (MICE) imputation. For time-series, use forward fill or interpolation. The best method depends on why the data is missing — if missingness is informative, consider adding a binary “was_missing” indicator feature alongside the imputation.

title: Week 5: Data Preprocessing and Regularization
text:
Overfitting & Why Regularization
The Problem: Overfitting

Model learns noise in training data → poor performance on unseen data
Solutions: more data, feature selection, or regularization

The Solution: Regularization

Adds a penalty term to the cost function that discourages large coefficients
Forces simpler models → better generalization to unseen data
Can also handle multicollinearity and perform feature selection

title: Week 5: Data Preprocessing and Regularization
text:
How Regularization Works
The optimization now balances two objectives:

Minimizing training error (original cost function)
Minimizing coefficient magnitudes (penalty term)

Three main types:

L2 (Ridge): Penalty = sum of squared coefficients
L1 (Lasso): Penalty = sum of absolute values of coefficients
Elastic Net: Combination of L1 and L2

Ridge, Lasso, and Elastic Net are regularized versions of linear regression — they modify its cost function by adding a penalty on the coefficients. The same idea applies to logistic regression and other linear models.

title: Week 5: Data Preprocessing and Regularization
text:
L2 Regularization (Ridge Regression)
\[J(\mathbf{w}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{p} w_j^2\]

Adds the sum of squared coefficients as a penalty
Shrinks coefficients toward zero but rarely makes them exactly zero
Good for handling multicollinearity
All features are kept in the model

title: Week 5: Data Preprocessing and Regularization
text:
L1 Regularization (Lasso Regression)
\[J(\mathbf{w}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{p} |w_j|\]

Adds the sum of absolute values of coefficients as a penalty
Can shrink coefficients to exactly zero → automatic feature selection
Useful when you suspect many features are irrelevant
Produces sparse models

title: Week 5: Data Preprocessing and Regularization
text:
Effect of the Regularization Parameter (\(\lambda\))

\(\lambda\) = 0: No regularization (same as ordinary least squares)
Small \(\lambda\): Mild penalty, coefficients shrunk slightly
Large \(\lambda\): Strong penalty, coefficients shrunk aggressively
\(\lambda\) → ∞: All coefficients approach zero

Key difference as \(\lambda\) increases:

L2 (Ridge): Coefficients shrink toward zero but rarely become exactly zero
L1 (Lasso): Coefficients can become exactly zero → automatic feature selection

title: Week 5: Data Preprocessing and Regularization
text:
L1 vs. L2 Regularization
L1 (Lasso): Tends to produce sparse models (many coefficients are zero).

Performs feature selection, but can be less stable than L2.

L2 (Ridge): Shrinks all coefficients towards zero, but rarely makes them exactly zero.

More stable than L1 and does not perform feature selection.

text:
Elastic Net
\[J(\mathbf{w}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 + \lambda_1 \sum_{j=1}^{p} |w_j| + \lambda_2 \sum_{j=1}^{p} w_j^2\]

l1_ratio = 1 → pure Lasso (L1)

Useful when there are correlated features (Lasso may arbitrarily pick one)

title: Week 5: Data Preprocessing and Regularization
section: Regularization in Logistic Regression: The C Parameter
text:
Regularization in Logistic Regression: The C Parameter
Scikit-learn’s LogisticRegression uses C = 1/\(\lambda\) (inverse of regularization strength)

Large C (e.g., 100) = weak regularization (small \(\lambda\)) → complex model
Small C (e.g., 0.01) = strong regularization (large \(\lambda\)) → simpler model

Key parameters in LogisticRegression():

C: regularization strength (default = 1.0)
penalty: ‘l1’, ‘l2’ (default), ‘elasticnet’, or ‘none’
l1_ratio: mixing parameter when penalty=‘elasticnet’ (0 = pure L2, 1 = pure L1)

Note: Ridge/Lasso use alpha (= \(\lambda\)), but LogisticRegression uses C (= 1/\(\lambda\))

title: Week 5: Data Preprocessing and Regularization
text:
Regularization: Summary & Key Takeaways

What it does: Prevents overfitting by penalizing large coefficients
Three methods:

L2 (Ridge): shrinks all coefficients, handles multicollinearity
L1 (Lasso): can zero out coefficients → feature selection
Elastic Net: combines L1 + L2 (use l1_ratio to control the mix)

Parameters: Ridge/Lasso use alpha (=\(\lambda\)); LogisticRegression uses C (=1/\(\lambda\))
When to use: High-dimensional data, overfitting, multicollinearity
How to tune: Cross-validation + grid/random search
Always: Scale features before applying regularization!

# Perform grid search with cross-validation using accuracy as the scoring metric

# Print the best parameter and corresponding cross-validation accuracy

Why is Machine Learning Important Today?

Explosion of data (Big Data)
Increased computing power
Advancements in algorithms
Demand for automation and intelligent systems
Wide range of applications


Big Data refers to the immense and rapidly growing volumes of structured and unstructured data generated by the internet, mobile devices, and sensors. The amount of data available today is unprecedented, and this scale creates demand for automated systems that can analyze data efficiently and extract useful knowledge.
Powerful machine learning algorithms often require significant computational resources because training is iterative and data-intensive. Recent hardware advances, including powerful processors and cloud computing platforms, make it possible to train complex models more efficiently. This increased computational power is essential for handling large datasets and the complex calculations required by machine learning models.

Machine Learning vs. Traditional Programming







Traditional Programming
Machine Learning




Programmer writes explicit rules.
Algorithm learns rules from data.


Input data + rules → output results.
Input data + desired outputs → learned model.


Best when logic is known and stable.
Best when patterns are complex or hard to hand-code.




Traditional programming means writing explicit rules that the computer follows. A calculator app is a clear example: the programmer writes instructions for addition, subtraction, and every other supported operation. This works well when the rules are known.
Machine learning is useful when the rules are too complex to write by hand. Face recognition is a good example: instead of hand-coding every possible relationship between eyes, nose, jawline, lighting, and pose, we give the system many labeled examples and let it learn patterns.
Examples that illustrate this distinction include Google Translate learning from translated sentences, medical imaging systems learning diagnostic patterns from scans, and recommendation systems such as Spotify Discover Weekly learning from user behavior. The takeaway is that traditional programming is best when rules are known, while machine learning is useful when the rules are complex, numerous, or unknown.

Unsupervised Learning

Goal: discover hidden patterns, structures, and relationships.
Examples: customer segmentation, anomaly detection, dimensionality reduction.

Unsupervised Learning: Example


Task: Group similar customers together.

Features: customer demographics, purchase history, etc.
Model: K-means clustering.






K-means clustering starts by choosing the number of clusters, K. It initializes cluster centroids, often randomly or with K-means++, then assigns each data point to the nearest centroid using a distance measure such as Euclidean distance. The centroids are updated as the mean of the points assigned to each cluster. Assignment and update steps repeat until the centroids stop changing significantly or a maximum number of iterations is reached.

Reinforcement Learning
An agent learns to interact with an environment by taking actions and receiving rewards.

Goal: learn an optimal policy, a sequence of actions that maximizes cumulative reward.
Examples: game playing, robotics, resource management, reasoning models.

The Machine Learning Workflow


1 Problem Definition


2 Data Collection & Preparation


3 Model Selection


4 Training


5 Evaluation


6 Tuning


7 Deployment

Step 1: Problem Definition

Clearly define the problem you want to solve.
What are your goals and objectives?
What type of ML problem is it?

Classification
Regression
Clustering

What data do you need?


Clearly define the problem you want to solve. Think of it as asking a clear question: for example, an online shop might ask, “Can I identify new customers likely to stop buying so I can send them a discount before they leave?”
Define what success means. For a cat-vs-dog photo classifier, a goal might be to label at least 9 out of 10 photos correctly. Also identify the problem type: predicting tomorrow’s temperature is regression, deciding whether email is spam is classification, and grouping similar news articles without labels is clustering.
Finally, decide what data is needed. If predicting whether a student passes an exam, useful features might include study hours, attendance, and previous grades. If those are not available, data collection becomes part of the project.

Step 2: Data Collection and Preparation

Gather data from various sources.
Clean and preprocess the data:

handle missing values
detect outliers
scale features
transform data

Split data into training, validation, and testing sets.


Data collection gathers the raw information the model will learn from. For a weather prediction task, this might include temperature, humidity, wind speed, historical records, and satellite images.
Real-world data is usually messy. Missing values may need to be filled or removed. Outliers, such as a house price entered as $1 when most prices are between $100K and $500K, should be investigated. Feature scaling keeps variables with large numeric ranges from dominating smaller-scale features. Data transformation converts fields such as color names into numeric representations the model can use.
Split data into training, validation, and test sets. For 1,000 labeled photos, a typical split might use 700 for training, 150 for validation, and 150 held out for final testing.

Step 3: Model Selection
Choose an appropriate ML algorithm based on the problem and data.
Consider:

type of problem: supervised or unsupervised
data characteristics
interpretability
computational resources


Choose the algorithm based on the problem and data. If predicting whether a student passes or fails, logistic regression may be a good starting point. For recognizing handwritten digits, a neural network may be more suitable.
Consider whether the problem is supervised or unsupervised, the size and shape of the data, whether the result must be interpretable, and the available computational resources. A doctor may need a model whose decision can be explained, while a large image-recognition task may justify a more complex model and GPU resources.

Step 4: Model Training

Feed the training data to the chosen algorithm.
The algorithm learns patterns and relationships in the data.
Model parameters are adjusted to minimize the error or loss function.


Model training is where learning happens. For example, teaching a model to recognize apples and oranges is like showing many labeled examples and letting the model discover the distinguishing patterns.
The model adjusts its internal parameters to reduce prediction error. If it predicts “apple” when the label is “orange”, the loss function measures the error and training updates the model to make fewer mistakes next time.

Step 5: Model Evaluation

Assess the model’s performance on validation/test data.
Use appropriate evaluation metrics:

accuracy
precision
recall
F1-score
mean squared error (MSE)

Determine whether the model meets the desired performance goals.


Evaluation tests the model on data it has not seen during training. If a cat-vs-dog classifier correctly labels 140 out of 150 held-out photos, that is about 93% accuracy and gives an estimate of real-world performance.
Different problems need different metrics. Accuracy can be misleading for rare diseases: a model that always predicts “no cancer” may be highly accurate but useless. Precision, recall, and F1-score help reveal performance on important cases. Compare the result to the goals from problem definition before deciding whether to continue or iterate.

Step 6: Model Tuning

Fine-tune model hyperparameters to improve performance.
Use techniques like cross-validation to find good hyperparameter settings.
Iterate between training, evaluation, and tuning.


Hyperparameters are settings selected before training. For a decision tree, maximum depth is a hyperparameter: a shallow tree may underfit, while a very deep tree may memorize the training data.
Cross-validation tests models more reliably by rotating which fold of the data is used for validation. Tuning is iterative: train, evaluate, adjust settings, retrain, and keep the setting that improves validation performance without overfitting.

Step 7: Model Deployment

Integrate the trained model into a real-world application or system.
Monitor model performance over time.
Retrain the model periodically with new data.


Deployment moves the model from a notebook experiment into a real system. A movie recommendation model, for example, runs behind the scenes in a streaming app and produces personalized recommendations for users.
A deployed model must be monitored because the world changes. A clothing recommender trained on winter behavior may perform poorly in summer, and spam filters must adapt to new spam patterns. Retraining with fresh data keeps the model current.

Simple Linear Regression


\[
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \epsilon
\]

\(\beta_1\) slope: how much \(y\) changes for a one-unit increase in \(x\)
\(\beta_0\) intercept: value of \(y\) when \(x=0\)
\(\epsilon\) error: part of \(y\) not explained by the line
Goal: find \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) that minimize error
\(x\) is the feature; \(y\) is the target

Fitting via Least Squares


Objective: minimize the sum of squared residuals.
\[
S(\beta_0,\beta_1)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left(y_i-(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)\right)^2
\]
Set the partial derivatives to zero to solve for the coefficients.


Closed-form solution
\[
\hat{\beta}_1 =
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}
{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})^2}
\]
\[
\hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y}-\hat{\beta}_1\bar{x}
\]



Derivation of the least-squares estimators: We want to fit the model \(y=\beta_0+\beta_1x\) to \(n\) data points. Define \(S(\beta_0,\beta_1)=\sum_i [y_i-(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i)]^2\) and minimize it by taking partial derivatives with respect to \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\).
For \(\beta_0\), \(\partial S/\partial \beta_0=-2\sum_i[y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i]=0\). Dividing by \(-2\) and expanding gives \(\sum_i y_i-n\beta_0-\beta_1\sum_i x_i=0\). Divide by \(n\) to get \(\bar{y}-\beta_0-\beta_1\bar{x}=0\), so \(\beta_0=\bar{y}-\beta_1\bar{x}\).
For \(\beta_1\), \(\partial S/\partial \beta_1=-2\sum_i x_i[y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i]=0\). Substitute \(\beta_0=\bar{y}-\beta_1\bar{x}\), collect terms, and use the identities \(\sum_i(x_i-\bar{x})^2=\sum_i x_i^2-n\bar{x}^2\) and \(\sum_i(x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})=\sum_i x_iy_i-n\bar{x}\bar{y}\). The result is \(\beta_1=\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}{\sum_i(x_i-\bar{x})^2}\) and \(\beta_0=\bar{y}-\beta_1\bar{x}\). This also shows the fitted line passes through \((\bar{x},\bar{y})\).

Model Evaluation Metrics


Mean Squared Error
\[
\mathrm{MSE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2
\]
Average squared error. Lower values mean predictions are closer to the observed targets.


Coefficient of Determination
\[
R^2 = 1 -
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2}
{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\bar{y})^2}
\]
Proportion of target variance explained by the model. Closer to 1 is better.



MSE gives one number for how wrong the model is on average. Raw prediction errors can cancel each other, so we square them first. Squaring also penalizes large errors more heavily. Lower MSE is better, but the value is in squared target units, so its meaning depends on the scale of the problem.
\(R^2\) asks how much better the model is than simply predicting the mean target every time. The numerator is unexplained variation and the denominator is total variation in \(y\). An \(R^2\) of 1.0 is a perfect fit, 0.8 means the model explains about 80% of the variance, 0.0 means it is no better than the mean baseline, and negative values can occur on test data when the model is worse than the mean baseline.

Introduction to Gradient Descent

Gradient Descent


Gradient descent is an iterative method for minimizing a cost function.


Initialize
Choose starting parameter values.


Compute gradients
Measure the direction of steepest increase.


Update parameters
Move in the opposite direction.


Repeat
Continue until convergence.

Gradient Descent Algorithm Steps


Update rule
\[
\beta_j \leftarrow \beta_j -
\alpha\frac{\partial J(\boldsymbol{\beta})}{\partial \beta_j}
\]

\(\alpha\) is the learning rate.
\(J(\boldsymbol{\beta})\) is the cost function, usually MSE for linear regression.
Stop when changes are small or maximum iterations are reached.



The update is applied to every parameter:
\[
\beta_0,\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_p
\]
The learning rate controls how large each step is along the cost surface.

Partial Derivative of Cost Function
For simple linear regression:
\[
\hat{y}_i = \beta_0+\beta_1x_i
\]


MSE cost
\[
J(\beta_0,\beta_1)=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}
(y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2
\]


Gradients
\[
\frac{\partial J}{\partial \beta_0}
=-\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\hat{y}_i)
\]
\[
\frac{\partial J}{\partial \beta_1}
=-\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i(y_i-\hat{y}_i)
\]

A good residual plot should look randomly scattered around zero. Any discernible pattern implies the model is missing some aspect of the underlying relationship. The pattern can guide refinements such as adding polynomial terms, addressing heteroscedasticity, accounting for periodicity, or including additional features.
Once the coefficients are obtained, compare them with domain expertise. If they contradict established understanding without a plausible explanation, treat that as a red flag and investigate the model, data, or feature design.

Practical Considerations


Feature Scaling
Helps optimization converge faster and more stably, especially when features have very different units.


Initialization
Affects how quickly, or whether, gradient-based methods converge.


Regularization
Balances bias and variance, prevents overfitting, and keeps coefficients in check.



\[
x_{\text{scaled}}=\frac{x-x_{\min}}{x_{\max}-x_{\min}}
\qquad
x_{\text{standardized}}=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}
\]


Feature scaling matters because features with very different scales can slow down gradient descent. Normalization or standardization makes the optimization problem better conditioned and often more numerically stable. Always fit the scaler on the training set only, then apply it to training and test data.
Initialization is less critical for simple linear regression because the cost surface is convex, but it matters more in complex models such as neural networks. Zero or small random values are often sufficient for linear models; neural networks may use schemes such as Xavier/Glorot or He initialization.
Regularization helps avoid overfitting and can make coefficients more stable and interpretable. Ridge uses an L2 penalty, \(\lambda\sum_j\theta_j^2\); Lasso uses an L1 penalty, \(\lambda\sum_j|\theta_j|\); Elastic Net combines both. Use cross-validation to choose \(\lambda\) and monitor both training and validation or test performance.

Overfitting & Underfitting


Overfitting
The model has too much flexibility and fits noise.
Remedies

Regularization: L1, L2, Elastic Net
Early stopping for iterative methods
Collect more data
Simplify the model
Cross-validation for hyperparameters



Underfitting
The model is too simple to capture the signal.
Remedies

Use polynomial terms or additional features
Reduce overly strong regularization
Apply feature engineering
Compare train, validation, and test metrics
Monitor metrics during development

Why Train-Test Split?


The problem: overfitting

A model can memorize training data instead of learning patterns.
Evaluating only on training data gives an overly optimistic score.
We need to test on data the model has never seen before.



The solution: train-test split

Split data into training set, about 70-80%, and test set, about 20-30%.
Train only on the training set.
Evaluate on the held-out test set.
Test score estimates generalization to new data.

Train-Test Split in scikit-learn


from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.5, random_state=42
)

lr_model = LinearRegression()
lr_model.fit(X_train, y_train)

train_score = lr_model.score(X_train, y_train)
test_score = lr_model.score(X_test, y_test)

print("Train R^2:", train_score)
print("Test R^2:", test_score)


Use train_test_split to separate data.
Compare train and test \(R^2\) to detect overfitting or underfitting.
